newsitem.title: UK: S&P raises Jordan's long-term rating to BB minus.
newsitem.headline: S&P raises Jordan's long-term rating to BB minus.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Thursday it raised its long-term foreign currency rating on the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan to BB minus, and has revised the outlook on the rating to stable from positive.
In addition, S&P said it affirmed its BBB minus long-term and A3 short-term ratings on Jordan's dinar-denominated debt.
"The outlook on the local currency rating remains stable," it said in a statement.

S&P said it had also assigned its BB minus rating to the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan's Brady bonds, totaling US$745 million, including US$494 million in par bonds due 2023, US$157 million in discount bonds due 2023, and US$94 million in past due interest bonds due 2023.

"The upgrade is based on progress in strengthening public finances, underpinned by a strong commitment to fiscal restraint, which is reducing Jordan's vulnerability to adverse external economic and political developments," S&P said.

"Adherence to an ambitious IMF-sponsored economic adjustment programme, renewed earlier this year until 1998, should ensure that Jordan's still-weak external payments and foreign exchange positions continue to improve."
"A low external debt service burden, projected at 14 to-15 percent of exports over the next two to three years, also supports the upgrade," S&P said.
S&P said deepening fiscal reforms were expected to keep budget out turns in small surplus for the fifth and sixth consecutive years in 1996 and 1997.
"This, in turn, should sustain the downward trend in the public debt burden," said S&P.

"Supported by ongoing microeconomic reforms and an increasingly stable regional environment, robust export growth is expected to contain current account deficits to under three percent of GDP annually during 1996/1997," the agency said.
"Coupled with likely additional debt relief from official creditors next year, modest external imbalances gradually should raise Jordan's low foreign exchange reserves," S&P said.

S&P said the investment-grade local currency rating reflected the low stock of dinar debt (about 17 percent of GDP this year), the interest payments on which absorb only one percent of government revenues.
"The central bank's demonstrated ability to contain inflation to single digits, even during periods of acute political and financial stress, also underpins the higher dinar rating," said S&P.
S&P said Jordan's ratings were constrained by the following.

-- A favorably structured, but heavy, gross government debt burden, which, at 122 percent of GDP in 1996, is the highest among similarly rated sovereigns, and limits fiscal and external payments flexibility.
-- The low level of foreign exchange reserves, the most liquid portion of which is equivalent to under two months of imports and remain vulnerable to balance of payments pressures
-- A dependence on remittances, tourism receipts, and intra-regional trade, which are sensitive to potential setbacks in the peace process.

"The outlook balances the commitment to disciplined fiscal and monetary policies, with still-limited financial flexibility, and the challenge of advancing fiscal reforms as high unemployment persists," said S&P.

It said recent disturbances which followed increases in bread prices posed little near-term threat to the government and to domestic stability owing to King Hussein's popularity and strong political position.
"However uncertainties surrounding the resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict pose risks to Jordan's balance of payments, and its internal and external security over the long term," S&P said.
